I am 49 years old. I have been farming these fields in Quzhou since I was a teenager. I never went to school, but I know this land and this climate better than any book ever could. My family has about 6 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and every year I follow the rotation my father taught me: winter wheat followed by summer maize. It is the only system I trust. The wheat goes in after National Day, around early October, and comes off the field in early June before the rains get heavy. Then I plant maize the same day we finish wheat harvest — there is no time to waste. For wheat, I rotary-till the land to break up the stubble and level the field. I sow "luyuan502" — it is an improved variety that my neighbors all use, and it gives steady yields without too much trouble. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea at green-up and jointing. Water is getting harder to find every year, so I irrigate three times: once before winter to protect the seedlings from freezing, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once at grain filling. I spray insecticide twice, herbicide once after sowing, and fungicide once when the weather turns humid. I expect about 1000 jin per mu if the weather cooperates.

For the summer maize, I do not till the soil at all — there is no time, and the wheat stubble helps keep moisture in. I plant "denghai605," a hybrid seed that the dealer in town promises is good. I apply less fertilizer for maize than for wheat, mostly at sowing and a small topdressing when the plants are knee-high. I irrigate twice: once right after sowing to help emergence, and once at the big trumpet stage. I spray insecticide twice and herbicide once; I usually do not bother with fungicide on maize unless I see something wrong. The maize normally yields about 1100 jin per mu, sometimes more if the August rains come on time.

I do not experiment with cotton or vegetables like some younger farmers. Those crops need too much labor and the prices jump around. Wheat and maize have government minimum purchase prices, and I can sell them at the grain station without worrying. My land is small, but this rotation feeds my family and leaves a little cash for the year.
